pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Compare and order numbers to 1000 with >, =, < by reasoning from the highest place down: compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones. Directly extends the two-digit 'tens-first' rule to a three-place, most-significant-digit-first procedure.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'compare and order numbers up to 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.4 'compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits, using >, =, and < symbols'.
• Operational details — Generalise 'compare the biggest place first' to three columns using aligned builds and a place-value chart; only drop to the next column when the current column ties. Stress-test with same-hundreds pairs (352 vs 358), digit-swap traps (352 vs 325) and different-length comparisons (99 vs 100). Move from pairs to ordering sets and to number-line placement.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): compares three-digit numbers with different hundreds using a build. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): orders a set to 1000 and states 'hundreds first, then tens, then ones'. Tier C (age 8, extending): resolves same-hundreds and mixed-length cases and justifies via place value, not digit count.
bestPractices: Generalise the rule to 'compare the highest place first, move down only on a tie' — same reasoning as two-digit, one more column.
Align builds/columns so the child scans hundreds→tens→ones and sees where the decision is made.
Use same-hundreds pairs (352/358) and digit-swaps (352/325) so the ordering can't be done by eyeballing.
Include mixed-length comparisons (99 vs 100) to defeat 'more digits sometimes / bigger ones digit' errors via place value.
Progress pair → ordered set → number line to connect comparison with magnitude.
keyRepresentations: Aligned base-ten builds / place-value counters in H|T|O columns
commonMisconceptions: Comparing ones or the biggest single digit instead of hundreds first (358 > 372 because 8 > 2).
'More digits = bigger' misapplied, or failing 99 vs 100 by digit count reasoning done wrongly.
Not descending to the next column when the hundreds tie.
Reversing the symbol or binding it to page order.
Ignoring internal zeros when comparing (305 vs 350).

learn.summary: Ages 7-8 compare and order numbers up to 1000 using >, =, < by reasoning from the highest place down: compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones, descending a column only when the current one ties and stopping at the first place where the digits differ. This extends the two-digit 'tens-first' rule to three places. Core practice uses aligned place-value builds with a left-to-right scan, trap pairs (same-hundreds, digit-swap, mixed-length, internal-zero), set ordering, and number-line placement.

activities.title: Scan the places left-to-right with two aligned builds
feedback: If a learner judges 358 > 372 because 8 > 2, point back to the hundreds: 3 hundreds vs 3 hundreds tie, so move to the tens where 5 < 7, so 358 < 372.
When the hundreds tie (352 vs 358), prompt: 'Hundreds are equal, so which place decides next?' then compare the tens, then the ones.
For 99 vs 100, align by place: 100 has 1 hundred while 99 has 0 hundreds, so 100 is larger. The extra digit matters because it stands for a higher place.
For 305 vs 350, highlight the internal zero: hundreds tie, then compare the tens (0 vs 5), so 305 < 350.
If the reasoning is right but the symbol is reversed, re-anchor: the open side faces the larger number; read the whole statement aloud to check.
activities.rationale: Comparison to 1000 is a left-to-right decision procedure; acting on aligned builds and scanning H→T→O makes visible where the decision is settled and generalises the known two-digit rule by adding one column.
sourceClaims: Compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens and ones digits, using >, =, < (2.NBT.4).
Comparison generalises as a most-significant-digit-first procedure; mixed-length and same-leading-digit cases target common errors.
learnerActions: Build or view two numbers (e.g. 352 and 358) as aligned base-ten builds or counters in H | T | O columns.
Place a >, =, or < card between them, with the open side facing the larger number.
Work left to right: decide at the hundreds first; only if the hundreds tie, move to the tens; only if the tens tie, move to the ones. Stop at the first place where the digits differ.
Say aloud which place settled the decision and why.
Repeat with trap pairs: same-hundreds (352 vs 358), digit-swap (352 vs 325), and mixed-length (99 vs 100).
Then order a set of 4-5 numbers smallest to largest and place numbers on a 0-1000 number line.
activities.intendedInsight: When the numbers are lined up by place, the comparison is always decided at the first (highest) place where the two numbers differ; move down to the next place only on a tie. A bigger ones digit does not by itself make a number larger. A whole number with more digits (and no leading zeros) is larger because it reaches a higher place, as when 100 has a hundred and 99 does not.

activities.title: Consolidation: choose the symbol, order a set, make it true
feedback: If a trap pair is answered by the ones digit, re-run the left-to-right scan from the hundreds.
After ordering a set, ask the learner to justify one adjacent pair by naming the deciding place.
On the number line, check that placement agrees with the symbol choice — larger numbers sit further right.
activities.rationale: Comparison and ordering map directly to scorable item formats, which are well suited to consolidating and checking the procedure once the scan is understood. This format exercises the rule rather than first scaffolding it.
learnerActions: Choose the correct >, =, or < for pairs including trap cases such as 358 vs 372 and 305 vs 350.
Order a set of five numbers up to 1000 from smallest to largest.
Fill a blank to make a comparison statement true (e.g. choose a tens digit that makes '3_6 > 352' true).
Place a given number on a 0-1000 number line (slider or marked rail).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent, reliable application of hundreds-first comparison across varied pairs and sets, connecting comparison to magnitude on a number line.

activities.title: Annotated worked reference for the scan
feedback: Prompt the learner to name the first place that differs in each annotated example.
After reading, ask them to predict and then check a new pair using the same steps.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated example gives a stable reference for the procedure and vocabulary; it supports but does not replace practice across many varied pairs, which develops fluency.
learnerActions: Step through a static annotated comparison such as 352 vs 358: see 'hundreds equal → look at the tens → 5 = 5 tie → look at the ones → 8 > 2, so 358 is larger'.
Read the caption that states the rule: compare the highest place first; move down only on a tie; stop at the first place that differs.
Re-state the rule in your own words before trying fresh pairs.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference model of the left-to-right scan and the stopping condition that learners can return to.

activities.title: Convince-me: rebut a wrong comparison
feedback: If the learner only restates the answer, ask them to name which place proves it and why the ones digit does not decide.
Accept any correct justification that identifies the first differing place and the correct order.
activities.rationale: Articulating and defending the reasoning surfaces whether the learner understands the stopping condition rather than reciting a surface rule. The underlying skill is procedural, so pair this with hands-on comparison practice.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who claims 358 > 372 'because 8 is bigger than 2'.
Explain why the claim is wrong, using the hundreds-then-tens reasoning, and state the correct comparison.
Construct a short justification: 'Hundreds tie, so look at the tens; 5 < 7, so 358 < 372.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify a comparison in words — not just get the symbol right — strengthens the place-value reasoning behind the procedure.

constraints: UK DfE National Curriculum, Year 3: 'compare and order numbers up to 1000'. US CCSS-M 2.NBT.4: compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens and ones digits using >, =, <.

Include same-hundreds pairs (352/358), digit-swap traps (352/325) and mixed-length comparisons (99/100) so learners cannot order by eyeballing or by the ones digit. For mixed-length pairs, link the extra digit to the higher place it represents.
Progress from single pairs to ordering a set to number-line placement to connect comparison with magnitude.
Right-align numbers by place before comparing; include internal-zero cases (305 vs 350).
A static annotated reference models the procedure but does not substitute for practice across many varied pairs; use it as a scaffold.

Scorable item formats (choose-the-symbol, order-the-set, fill-the-blank, number-line slider) are well suited to consolidation and checking; they exercise the procedure and do not by themselves scaffold the initial left-to-right scan.
The 'convince-me' dialogue targets justification; because the skill is procedural, keep it paired with hands-on comparison practice rather than using it alone.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

CCSS-M 2.NBT.4 and the NCETM claim are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE Year 3 claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is carried over as-is and not independently confirmed here.

Per-activity sourceClaims were trimmed to retain a claim only where it directly supports that activity's teaching principle. The DfE claim is topic/objective-level and was removed from all per-activity lists (it remains cited in constraints as the standard). The NCETM/CCSS claims were retained only on activity 1, whose rationale is the comparison procedure itself; activities 2-4 were set to [] because their rationales concern medium/method affordances (consolidation formats, reference model, dialogue justification) that the retained claims do not directly establish, even though those activities use the same comparison content.

The legacy '3D adds nothing' universal for magnitude ordering is not established by the source evidence and was dropped; 'not proposed in 3D here' is not the same as 'impossible'. Ordering is well represented in 2D/number-line form.

Legacy 'ideal'/'self-correcting'/'engineered moment of insight' framing implied the interactive bench uniquely achieves the effect; this has been softened to an observable affordance (a visible left-to-right scan) without asserting superiority over other media.

Assessment-field examples (254 vs 245 turns on the tens; 73 among 137/307/370) were checked and are consistent with hundreds-then-tens-then-ones reasoning, but were not independently re-verified against sources.

probeDeeper: Which place did you compare first — and why the hundreds?
254 and 245 — which is bigger, and how did you decide?
Where does 73 go among the three-digit numbers, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 254 > 245; order 73, 137, 307, 370; comparing hundreds first, then tens, then ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares from the ones, or by a bigger digit anywhere, instead of hundreds-first: judges 254 vs 245 by the ones (says 245 is bigger)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare place by place from the hundreds; stop at the first place that differs (tens: 5 > 4).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The same-hundreds pair is ordered by the ones digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misorders 2- and 3-digit numbers by digit-count or first glance: places 73 above 137
errorPatterns.nextMove: Right-align by place; a number reaching the hundreds beats one that stops at tens. Line them up in columns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 73 is ordered as if larger than a three-digit number, or numbers aren't aligned by place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the < / > symbol despite correct reasoning
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor: the open side faces the larger number. Read the statement aloud to check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says which is bigger correctly but writes the symbol the wrong way round.

responseLevels.gap: Compares from the ones or by digit-count; symbol may be reversed.
responseLevels.full: Compares hundreds-then-tens-then-ones, orders numbers to 1000 reliably, and records with >, =, < correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Orders clearly different numbers but errs on same-hundreds pairs or mixed-length sets.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch them compare and order. 'Put a symbol between 254 and 245. Now order these smallest to largest: 307, 370, 73, 137. Tell me which place you looked at first.' The 254/245 pair turns on the tens, and 73 tests mixing 2- and 3-digit numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 254 vs 245 share hundreds and differ only at the tens, so a ones-first comparer picks wrongly; including 73 checks whether the child aligns by place rather than counting digits. Watching where they start (hundreds) exposes the method.
